ui.storyLede: Scientists studied urban streams in five European cities. These are their findings in their own words, with the page each one comes from. Between them, one short line of ours points you to real streams in the data.
ui.c2t: What a city does to a stream
ui.c4t: An early warning most monitoring misses
ui.c6t: And for fish, plants and animals
ui.s_c1: This app holds {n} of those research sites. {scored} have a published lab health-risk score, and {y} of those were sampled in 2023. Each stream page says how long ago that was.
ui.s_c2: Every stream page shows how its lab score compares with the other sites in the same city.
ui.s_c3: The lab score in this app combines pathogens, faecal contamination and antibiotic-resistance genes. It does not measure pharmaceuticals, so a low score does not rule them out.
ui.s_c4: Diatoms are not something a resident can check by eye. That is why the citizen check asks about what you can see, and why reports stay preliminary until someone reviews them.
ui.s_c5a: In this data, the highest antibiotic-resistance gene score is at
ui.s_c5b: ; the highest pathogen score is at
ui.s_c5c: {high} of the {scored} scored sites fall in our high third.
ui.s_c6: The citizen check asks about invasive plants and animals, bankside vegetation and water plants, because those are signs a resident can see.
ui.s_c7: Each stream page lists measures from OneAquaHealth's Catalogue of Measures, with the page number, so a resident or a city officer can see what has worked elsewhere.
ui.quoteEnglish: quoted in English; no official translation found for this sentence
ui.storyCta: Find a stream near you to see what was measured there and what it means for people, animals and the stream.
ui.storyNote: Quotes are copied verbatim from the OneAquaHealth Policy Brief and checked by script against the page cited. Lines marked StreamRecord are ours.
ui.quizIntro: Every answer is explained with the finding it comes from.
ui.q1: In how many of the monitored sites did OneAquaHealth detect pharmaceuticals?
ui.q1why: Sixteen different medicines turned up, often mixed together.
ui.q2b: In sites in good ecological condition
ui.q2c: Nowhere; it was the same everywhere
ui.q2why: Healthy streams soaked up part of the problem.
ui.q3: What do intact bankside plants do for a stream?
ui.q3b: Shade and cool the water, filter run-off, hold the banks and give wildlife a home
ui.q3why: This is why bankside vegetation is one of the questions in the check.
ui.homeStat: Pharmaceuticals were detected in 91% of monitored sites
ui.homeStatLine: OneAquaHealth found this in the streams of five European cities. Most people who live next to them have never been told what that means.
ui.nearbyTitle: Nearby streams with a lower lab score
ui.nearbyNote: Straight-line distance. These scores are from the same 2023 survey and are not a statement that any water is safe today.
ui.youIntro: Who are you here as? The reading changes to what matters for you.
ui.you_parent_high: Keep small children out of the water here. In 2023 this stream was in the highest third of lab health-risk scores: germs, sewage markers and antibiotic-resistance genes. Let them play by the stream, not in it, and wash their hands afterwards.
ui.you_parent_moderate: Let children play by the stream, not in it. In 2023 this stream was in the middle third of lab health-risk scores. Wash their hands afterwards, and never let them drink the water.
ui.you_parent_low: In 2023 this stream was in the lowest third of lab health-risk scores. That is the best of the sites tested, not a promise: water changes after rain. Keep small children from drinking it and wash their hands after play.
ui.you_parent_none: No lab result was published for this stream, so treat the water as untested. Let children play by it, not in it, and wash their hands afterwards.
ui.you_dog_high: Keep your dog out of the water and stop it drinking here. In 2023 this stream was in the highest third of lab health-risk scores. If your dog goes in, rinse its coat with clean water.
ui.you_dog_moderate: Do not let your dog drink from the stream. In 2023 it was in the middle third of lab health-risk scores. Rinse your dog with clean water after a swim.
ui.you_dog_low: In 2023 this stream was in the lowest third of lab health-risk scores. Even so, do not let your dog drink it, and keep it away from any green or blue-green scum.
ui.you_dog_none: No lab result was published for this stream. Treat the water as untested: do not let your dog drink it, and rinse it after a swim.
ui.you_walker_high: Walking here is fine; avoid touching the water, especially with cuts or grazes. In 2023 this stream was in the highest third of lab health-risk scores.
ui.you_walker_moderate: Walking here is fine. Avoid touching the water with cuts or grazes, and wash your hands before eating.
ui.you_walker_low: Walking here is fine, and OneAquaHealth links healthy urban streams to mental health benefits. Avoid drinking the water.
ui.you_walker_none: Walking here is fine. No lab result was published, so avoid touching the water with cuts and do not drink it.
ui.you_garden_high: Do not water vegetables or fruit you eat raw with this stream’s water. In 2023 it was in the highest third of lab health-risk scores, including sewage markers.
ui.you_garden_moderate: Do not use this stream’s water on vegetables or fruit you eat raw. In 2023 it was in the middle third of lab health-risk scores.
ui.you_garden_low: In 2023 this stream was in the lowest third of lab health-risk scores. Still, do not water vegetables you eat raw with untreated stream water.
ui.you_garden_none: No lab result was published for this stream. Do not water vegetables you eat raw with untreated stream water.
ui.you_gp: The clinician reading puts the lab record, what residents reported and what it may and may not indicate on one printable page.

foam.q: Is there foam on the water?
foam.hint: Look along the edges and behind stones.

colourSmell.q: Does the water look or smell unusual?
colourSmell.hint: For example an odd colour, a sewage or chemical smell, or rotten eggs.

riparianVegetation.q: How much of the bank is covered by trees and plants?
riparianVegetation.hint: Look along about 10 metres of bank on your side.

macrophytes.q: How much of the stream bed has water plants growing in it?
macrophytes.hint: Look into the water where you can see the bottom.

invasiveOrganisms.q: Do you see plants or animals that don't belong here?
invasiveOrganisms.hint: For example giant hogweed, Japanese knotweed or crayfish you don't recognise.

other.q: Do you notice any of these?

a.standingWater: Pools of still water by the stream

waterTemperature.q: Water temperature, if you have a thermometer
waterTemperature.hint: Optional. In degrees Celsius. Skip if you don't have one.

overallAssessment.hint: Your own view, now that you have looked closely. These are the OneAquaHealth app’s three answers.

a.GOOD: Good: the parts of a healthy stream are there: bankside plants, a natural channel, good water, wildlife
a.MODERATE: Moderate: some changes, but still full of life, with plants on the banks and water that looks good
a.POOR: Poor: heavily modified or concreted, bankside plants and habitats lost, polluted

feelings.hint: Choose any. OneAquaHealth asks this to link the health of a stream to how people feel near it.

foam.label: Foam on the water
foam.people: Avoid touching or swallowing the water. Wash your hands before eating.
foam.animals: Keep dogs out of the water and stop them licking foam from their coat. Birds and fish live with whatever caused it.
foam.stream: Persistent foam can come from detergents or waste water. A sign the stream may be receiving pollution.

clin.may: Foam is often natural, from decaying plant matter. Persistent white foam with a soapy or perfumed smell points to detergents or untreated waste water entering the stream.
clin.not: It does not tell you whether harmful microbes or chemicals are present, or at what level.
clin.advice: Avoid skin contact and swallowing water. Wash hands, and cover cuts. Keep dogs out of the water, stop them drinking it or licking foam from their coat, and rinse them with clean water after contact.
clin.contact: Report persistent foam, foam with a sewage or detergent smell, or foam with dead fish to the municipality. See a vet if a dog vomits, has diarrhoea or seems unwell after contact. A patient with symptoms after contact should mention the exposure to their GP.

colourSmell.label: Unusual colour or smell
colourSmell.people: Do not paddle or swim, and keep children out. Wash hands before eating.
colourSmell.animals: Keep dogs on a lead and out of the water. Low oxygen can stress fish and the insects birds feed on.
colourSmell.stream: Unusual colour or smell can mean waste water, a spill or low oxygen from decaying matter.

clin.may: A sewage smell or discoloured water suggests waste-water discharge. A rotten-egg smell suggests hydrogen sulphide from decaying matter in low-oxygen water. A chemical smell may mean a spill.
clin.not: It cannot identify the source or confirm an infection or poisoning risk.
clin.advice: No swimming or paddling, especially for children. Avoid contact, wash hands before eating and cover cuts. Keep dogs on a lead and out of the water.
clin.contact: Report to the municipality the same day if you see a discharge or smell sewage or chemicals. Anyone with diarrhoea, vomiting, fever, or a skin or eye rash after contact should see their GP and mention the water.

scum.label: Green or blue-green scum
scum.people: No swimming. Keep children away from the water's edge.
scum.animals: Keep dogs well away: some blooms are toxic and can kill a dog quickly. Fish and birds can be harmed too.
scum.stream: Scum often means an algal or cyanobacterial bloom, usually fed by nutrient pollution and warm, still water.

clin.may: A green or blue-green surface scum suggests an algal or cyanobacterial bloom. Some cyanobacteria produce toxins that affect the liver, nerves and skin.
clin.not: You cannot tell a toxic bloom from a harmless one by looking. Only laboratory testing can.
clin.advice: No swimming or paddling. Do not swallow the water or let it reach the eyes. Keep dogs on a lead, stop them drinking or entering the water, and wash their coat with clean water straight away if they get wet.
clin.contact: Treat a dog with vomiting, drooling, weakness, trembling or collapse after contact as an emergency and go to a vet at once. Report the bloom to the municipality. A person with skin or eye irritation, vomiting or diarrhoea after contact should see their GP.

deadFish.label: Dead fish
deadFish.people: Do not touch or collect the fish. Keep children away.
deadFish.animals: Stop dogs eating or rolling on dead fish. The cause may still be affecting other wildlife.
deadFish.stream: Dead fish can mean very low oxygen, a toxic spill or disease. It is time-sensitive for sampling.

clin.may: Fish deaths can follow low oxygen in hot weather or after organic pollution, a toxic spill, or disease in the fish population.
clin.not: It does not establish the cause, or whether the water poses a risk to people.
clin.advice: Do not handle dead fish with bare hands, and wash hands after any contact with the water. Keep dogs away and stop them eating carcasses.
clin.contact: Report to the municipality or environment agency immediately, because samples need to be taken quickly. See a vet if a dog has eaten fish and becomes unwell.

riparianVegetation.label: Little vegetation on the bank
riparianVegetation.people: Less shade and greenery along the water. Banks may erode and be less safe to walk.
riparianVegetation.animals: Fewer places for birds to nest and for fish and insects to shelter.
riparianVegetation.stream: Bank vegetation shades and cools the water and filters run-off. Losing it weakens the stream's defences.

clin.may: Sparse bank vegetation usually reflects urban development, clearing or erosion, which reduces the stream's ability to filter run-off.
clin.not: It is an ecological indicator, not a direct health hazard.
clin.advice: No specific precaution. Take care on eroded banks, especially with children and dogs.
clin.contact: Mention it to the municipality as part of any restoration request. No medical or veterinary contact is needed for this finding alone.

invasiveOrganisms.label: Plants or animals that don't belong
invasiveOrganisms.people: Do not touch unknown plants. Some, like giant hogweed, can cause blistering burns in sunlight.
invasiveOrganisms.animals: Stop dogs chewing plants by the water. Invasive species can crowd out native fish, insects and plants.
invasiveOrganisms.stream: Invasive species change the stream's ecology and spread easily on boots, gear and paws.

clin.may: Invasive plants and animals suggest a disturbed ecosystem. A few invasive riparian plants, such as giant hogweed, cause phytophotodermatitis.
clin.not: Most invasive species pose no direct risk to human health. Seeing one does not mean the water is contaminated.
clin.advice: Avoid touching unfamiliar plants, wash skin promptly after contact and keep it out of the sun. Clean boots and gear before visiting another stream. Stop dogs chewing plants.
clin.contact: Report invasive species to the municipality. A person with blistering or a burn-like rash after contact with a plant, particularly after sun exposure, should see their GP.

macrophytes.label: Few water plants
macrophytes.animals: Water plants give fish, insects and snails food, shelter and places to breed.
macrophytes.stream: Few water plants can follow pollution, shading changes or dredging, and leave the stream less able to clean itself.

clin.may: Few aquatic plants can reflect pollution, sediment, heavy shading or channel works.
clin.not: It is an ecological indicator, not a direct health hazard.
clin.contact: Mention it to the municipality as part of any restoration request. No medical or veterinary contact is needed for this finding alone.

standingWater.label: Pools of still water
standingWater.people: Still water can breed mosquitoes. Cover up and use repellent at dusk.
standingWater.animals: Stop dogs drinking from stagnant pools, which can hold bacteria and parasites.
standingWater.stream: Pools by the stream can mean blocked flow or poor drainage, and they concentrate pollutants.

clin.may: Stagnant pools are mosquito breeding habitat and can concentrate microbes and pollutants.
clin.not: It does not show that disease-carrying mosquitoes are present.
clin.advice: Reduce bites with repellent and covering skin at dusk. Empty containers that hold water near homes. Stop dogs drinking from stagnant pools.
clin.contact: Report persistent pooling or many mosquito larvae to the municipality. A person with fever after many mosquito bites should see their GP and mention the exposure.
